old_entry.title: Chrono Trigger
old_entry.subtitle: Time Becomes a Map to Traverse
old_entry.summary: A fairground accident sends Crono across centuries, while combined attacks make the travelling party matter in battle.
body: Crono meets Marle at Guardia's Millennial Fair. They visit Lucca's Telepod demonstration, and a malfunction sends Marle into the past. Crono follows with her pendant. A public celebration becomes the doorway to a journey through different periods of the same planet, released by Square in 1995.

Prehistory, the medieval world and the distant future give the journey different surroundings and companions. The premise makes travelling through time a practical way of exploring a world. The collaboration brought together Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii, Final Fantasy creators and Akira Toriyama's character designs.

In battle, action gauges fill while enemies change position. Characters can combine their special Tech abilities into joint attacks. Waiting for another party member can therefore create a different opportunity from acting immediately. The people travelling together affect both the story's company and the choices available during a fight.

The game's development team included three designers that Square dubbed the "Dream Team": Hironobu Sakaguchi, creator of Square's Final Fantasy series; Yuji Horii, creator of Enix's Dragon Quest series; and Akira Toriyama, character designer of Dragon Quest and author of the Dragon Ball manga series. In addition, Takashi Tokita co-directed the game and co-wrote the scenario, Kazuhiko Aoki produced the game, while Masato Kato wrote most of the story.

editorial_features.title: Yasunori Mitsuda: choosing the sound first
editorial_features.summary: A score needs more than melodies.
body: Mitsuda remembered beginning a Super Famicom working day by searching for sounds. Using samplers such as the Akai S-3200 and E-MU EIII, he could spend hours listening through CDs before selecting material. The process complicates an account that begins and ends with writing a melody. A note's identity depended on the sound chosen to carry it. His recollection gives that preparation time a place in the work, making the eventual soundtrack the result of selection as well as composition and the limits of its playback hardware.

For later recording work, Mitsuda wanted a demo to communicate its intended texture. He selected sounds himself even though other specialists would adjust the finished recording. A convincing demo, he believed, also helped live musicians understand the standard he sought. He treated those early sounds as part of directing a session, communicating his expectations before the musicians began playing. The demonstration carried instructions that a bare sequence of pitches could not: how parts should meet, and what kind of weight or colour their combination should have.

Chrono Trigger changed who would handle the sound effects. Mitsuda recalled asking Sakaguchi for composing work, then arguing that his former duties needed a specialist. He contacted friends from school, including Yoshitaka Hirota. Their conversations continued through the project. The celebrated score thus belongs within a rearrangement of jobs, not a clean division between an inspired composer and an anonymous technical background. Somebody still had to make the other sounds work after Mitsuda moved towards music, and the interview gives that person a name and a relationship.

Mitsuda also rejected the idea that sound programming was work he simply disliked. He credited Minoru Akao alongside himself for improving the sound of Square's Super Famicom games. In another example, a scheduling conflict shifted his proposed composing role on Breath of Fire V towards production, while Hitoshi Sakimoto wrote the score and colleagues handled sound work. Those distinctions prevent a single familiar name from swallowing the credits. Composing, preparing timbres and supervising a team can overlap without becoming the same contribution to every project.

old_entry.summary: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams, known as Street Fighter Zero in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades.
body: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams, known as Street Fighter Zero in Japan, Asia, South America, and Oceania, is a 1995 fighting game developed and published by Capcom for arcades. It was the first all-new Street Fighter game produced by Capcom since 1991's Street Fighter II. Plotwise, it serves as a prequel to Street Fighter II and thus features younger versions of established characters, as well as characters from the original Street Fighter and Final Fight.

The game introduces several new features, expanding on the Super Combo system previously featured in Super Street Fighter II Turbo, with graphics drawn in a similar art style to the one Capcom employed in Darkstalkers and X-Men: Children of the Atom. After its arcade release, it was ported to PlayStation and Sega Saturn home consoles. Street Fighter Alpha received a mainly positive reception; it was followed up by Street Fighter Alpha 2 in 1996 as part of the Alpha sub-series.

old_entry.subtitle: Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi Turns Listening into a Machine for Changing Horror
old_entry.summary: On August 4, 1995 Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi arrived on Super Famicom.
body: On August 4, 1995 Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi arrived on Super Famicom. Six students tell unsettling stories to a school reporter, but the order in which they are heard and the player's choices alter routes, details and conclusions. The game uses photographs, text and sound to build everyday horror around corridors, clubs and school legends. Fear does not depend on constant action; it comes from the suspicion that a familiar story may branch simply because a different person told it in a different way.

The game uses digitised photographs in its in-game graphics. It was developed by Pandora Box, the studio founded by designer and scenario writer Takeo Iijima. Its characters and setting later became part of the Apathy visual- and sound-novel franchise.

In the game you play as a reporter for the school paper, writing a story about the 7 School Mysteries. Each mystery is told to you by one of 6 possible other students. As you make your way through each scenario, you are given choices which will change the outcome of the story and therefore your progression through the game. Including hidden stories, there are more than 50 possible scenarios in the game.

Gakkou de atta Kowai Hanashi S followed on PlayStation in 1996. It added improved graphics, full-motion video and further narrative paths. This version also lets players choose the gender of the main character.

story_headings: Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi Turns Listening into a Machine for Changing Horror

original_body: On August 4, 1995 Gakkō de Atta Kowai Hanashi arrived on Super Famicom. Six students tell unsettling stories to a school reporter, but the order in which they are heard and the player's choices alter routes, details and conclusions. The game uses photographs, text and sound to build everyday horror around corridors, clubs and school legends. Fear does not depend on constant action; it comes from the suspicion that a familiar story may branch simply because a different person told it in a different way.

The game uses photographs of actors and everyday locations rather than relying on overt fantasy imagery. The contrast between almost documentary pictures, text and sound makes corridors and classrooms believable precisely when the story starts to distort them. Audio creates a second layer of information. Music and effects can anticipate a change, confirm a response or give a situation identity, linking perception and control immediately. The result remains recognizable because form and function move together, without separating the idea from the way it is experienced.

Six storytellers offer different tales, and the order in which they are selected opens variations, events and endings. The structure turns a simple anthology into a combinatorial machine in which the player also constructs the emotional sequence of fear. The narrative works because it is not separated from action. Information, motives and relationships arrive through spaces, systems or behavior, letting what the player understands coincide with what the player is asked to do. The consequence can be felt in the overall rhythm of play, where a local decision changes how the player reads what came before and what follows.

Bathrooms, clubs, stairs and rooms after hours become narrative spaces because the game works with fears already attached to school life. It does not need a separate fantasy world; it changes the meaning of familiar places and leaves that meaning unsettled in memory. The story becomes stronger when a narrative element also produces a practical consequence. The player is not merely told what the conflict means, but must inhabit it, recognize its effects and react within the available rules. That relationship between rule and consequence helps explain why the detail is remembered beyond the technical context of its era.

old_entry.title: Command & Conquer
old_entry.summary: Command & Conquer (also known by the retronym Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn) is a real-time strategy video game developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1995.
body: Command & Conquer (also known by the retronym Command & Conquer: Tiberian Dawn) is a real-time strategy video game developed and published by Westwood Studios in 1995. Set in an alternate history, the game tells the story of a world war between two globalized factions: the Global Defense Initiative of the United Nations and a revolutionary militant organization called the Brotherhood of Nod, led by the mysterious Kane.

Westwood conceived Command & Conquer during the final stages of the development of Dune II, and it expands on ideas explored in that title. Inspired by the events of the era, particularly the Gulf War, the team gave the game a modern warfare setting. The game contains live-action full motion video cutscenes, which star Westwood employees and few professional actors, including Joseph D. Kucan, who plays Kane. The Nintendo 64 port was developed by Looking Glass Studios.

Command & Conquer was a commercial and critical success, selling over three million copies and winning numerous awards. It has been cited as one of the greatest games ever made, and the title that defined and popularized the real-time strategy genre. The game was the first in the Command & Conquer series, which sold 30 million copies by 2009. To mark the 12th anniversary of the franchise, Electronic Arts, the current publisher and owner of the series, released the game for free in 2007.
A remastered version of the game was released in 2020 as part of the Command & Conquer Remastered Collection.

On August 31, 2007 Electronic Arts opened the twelfth-anniversary celebration of Command & Conquer by making Command & Conquer Gold available as a free download in a Windows XP-compatible form. This is the event documented by the calendar, not a silent rewriting of the original game's first release. The initiative matters because it turns an anniversary into an act of access. Two ISO images, one for GDI and one for Nod, put back into circulation an RTS that helped make the genre more readable, theatrical and audiovisually aggressive. Inspired by the events of the era, particularly the Gulf War, the team gave the game a modern warfare setting. body: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). The player controls Yoshi dinosaurs on their quest to reunite baby Mario with his brother Luigi, who has been kidnapped by the wizard Kamek. Yoshi runs and jumps to reach the end of each level while solving puzzles and collecting items with Mario's help.

Having introduced the character in the previous Super Mario game, Super Mario World (1990), Nintendo decided to develop a game starring Yoshi, with the aim of making it more accessible. Yoshi's Island introduced his signature flutter jump and egg-spawning abilities. The marker-drawn art style was created by scanning hand-drawn pictures and approximating them pixel-by-pixel. Some special effects were powered by a new Super FX2 microchip.

Yoshi's Island is a 2D side-scrolling platform game. In the Super Mario series platform game tradition, the player controls Yoshi in run-and-jump gameplay. The player navigates between platforms and atop some foes en route to the end of the increasingly difficult levels. The player characters are Yoshis who take turns traveling through 48 levels across six worlds to rescue Baby Luigi and reunite the brothers. Yoshi also collects coins to earn extra lives and retains his long tongue from Super Mario World. The game centers more on "puzzle-solving and item-collecting" than other platformers, with hidden flowers and red coins to find. Levels include mines, ski jumps, and "the requisite fiery dungeons". Every fourth level (two in each world) is a boss fight against a large version of a previous foe.

In a style new to the series, the game has a coloring book aesthetic with "scribbled crayon" backgrounds. Expanding on his "trademark tongue" ability to swallow enemies, Yoshi, as the focus of the game, is given a new move set: the ability to "flutter jump", throw eggs, and transform. The flutter jump gives Yoshi a secondary boost when the player holds the jump button. It became his new "trademark move", similar to that of Luigi in Super Mario Bros. 2. Yoshi can also pound the ground from mid-air to bury objects or break through soft earth, and use his long tongue to grab enemies at a distance. Swallowed enemies can be spat as projectiles immediately or stored for later use as an egg. The player individually aims and fires the eggs at obstacles via a new targeting system. The eggs also bounce off of surfaces in the environment. Up to six eggs can be stored this way, and will trail behind the character. Yoshi can also eat certain items for power-up abilities. For instance, watermelons let Yoshi shoot seeds from his mouth like a machine gun, and fire enemies turn his mouth into a flamethrower. Other power-ups transform Yoshi into vehicles including cars, drills, helicopters, and submarines. A star power-up makes Baby Mario invulnerable and extra fast.

While Yoshi is "virtually invincible", if hit by an enemy, Baby Mario will float off his back in a bubble while a timer counts down to zero. When the timer expires, Koopas arrive to take Baby Mario and Yoshi loses a life. The player can replenish the timer by collecting small stars and power-ups. However, Yoshi can also lose a life instantly if he comes into contact with obstacles such as pits, spikes, lava, and thorns. Similar to Super Mario World, the player can hold a power-up in reserve, such as a "+10 star" (which adds ten seconds to the Baby Mario timer) or a "magnifying glass" (which reveals all hidden red coins in a level). These power-ups are acquired in several minigames. At the end of each level, the Yoshi relays Baby Mario to the successive Yoshi. If the player perfects all eight levels in each world by finishing with all flowers, red coins, and full 30 seconds on the timer, two hidden levels will unlock. There are three save slots on the cartridge.

After four years of development, Yoshi's Island was released in Japan in August 1995 and worldwide two months later. It sold more than four million copies. Critics described it as one of the greatest video games of all time, praising the art, sound, level design and gameplay. The art style and Yoshi's signature characteristics established the Yoshi series of spin-offs and sequels.

Yoshi's Island was the last Super Mario platformer before the series' transition to 3D gameplay, with no further 2D entries for over a decade. It was ported to the Game Boy Advance as Yoshi's Island: Super Mario Advance 3 in 2002; this version was rereleased for the Nintendo 3DS and the Wii U's Virtual Console. The original version was also released for the Super NES Classic Edition, and both versions for the Nintendo Classics service.

prior_records.summary: On August 5, 1995 Yoshi's Island arrived on Super Famicom in Japan and rejected the idea that a sequel merely had to be bigger or shinier.
body: On August 5, 1995 Yoshi's Island arrived on Super Famicom in Japan and rejected the idea that a sequel merely had to be bigger or shinier. Its crayon-like lines, distortions and illustrated backgrounds embrace a deliberately handmade look, while eggs, flutter jumps and Baby Mario change how every space is read. The game does not simply replace Mario with Yoshi. It builds another grammar, more elastic and tactile, in which aiming, movement and protection coexist inside the same sequence of actions.

Yoshi's Island chooses irregular outlines, soft colors and surfaces that resemble crayons and markers. The effect makes the Super Famicom less interested in imitating pre-rendered graphics and more like an animated sketchbook with its own visual rules. Visual identity becomes effective when it overlaps with function. A graphic detail can signal danger, depth or character without text, building a grammar that the player learns through action. The consequence can be felt in the overall rhythm of play, where a local decision changes how the player reads what came before and what follows.

Yoshi can swallow enemies, turn them into eggs and throw those projectiles along a controlled trajectory. Platforming therefore gains a second grammar inside movement: players choose position and angle, not only the timing of a jump. Movement therefore becomes a language for reading space. Speed, inertia, distance and timing tell the player where a body can go and what each trajectory will cost, often before any written explanation is needed. That relationship between rule and consequence helps explain why the detail is remembered beyond the technical context of its era.

When Yoshi is hit, Baby Mario floats away and a countdown begins under an insistent cry. Damage becomes a recoverable emergency: the player can correct the mistake by reacting quickly, turning protection into a question of rhythm. Audio creates a second layer of information. Music and effects can anticipate a change, confirm a response or give a situation identity, linking perception and control immediately. This coherence lets the game teach its logic through use, making the experience itself an explanation of the system.

paragraph_selection.original: Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island is a 1995 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). The player controls Yoshi dinosaurs on their quest to reunite baby Mario with his brother Luigi, who has been kidnapped by the wizard Kamek. Yoshi runs and jumps to reach the end of each level while solving puzzles and collecting items with Mario's help.

paragraph_selection.original: Having introduced the character in the previous Super Mario game, Super Mario World (1990), Nintendo decided to develop a game starring Yoshi, with the aim of making it more accessible. Yoshi's Island introduced his signature flutter jump and egg-spawning abilities. The marker-drawn art style was created by scanning hand-drawn pictures and approximating them pixel-by-pixel. Some special effects were powered by a new Super FX2 microchip.

paragraph_selection.body: Yoshi's Island is a 2D side-scrolling platform game. In the Super Mario series platform game tradition, the player controls Yoshi in run-and-jump gameplay. The player navigates between platforms and atop some foes en route to the end of the increasingly difficult levels. The player characters are Yoshis who take turns traveling through 48 levels across six worlds to rescue Baby Luigi and reunite the brothers. Yoshi also collects coins to earn extra lives and retains his long tongue from Super Mario World. The game centers more on "puzzle-solving and item-collecting" than other platformers, with hidden flowers and red coins to find. Levels include mines, ski jumps, and "the requisite fiery dungeons". Every fourth level (two in each world) is a boss fight against a large version of a previous foe.
paragraph_selection.heading: Exploring worlds and finding collectibles

paragraph_selection.body: In a style new to the series, the game has a coloring book aesthetic with "scribbled crayon" backgrounds. Expanding on his "trademark tongue" ability to swallow enemies, Yoshi, as the focus of the game, is given a new move set: the ability to "flutter jump", throw eggs, and transform. The flutter jump gives Yoshi a secondary boost when the player holds the jump button. It became his new "trademark move", similar to that of Luigi in Super Mario Bros. 2. Yoshi can also pound the ground from mid-air to bury objects or break through soft earth, and use his long tongue to grab enemies at a distance. Swallowed enemies can be spat as projectiles immediately or stored for later use as an egg. The player individually aims and fires the eggs at obstacles via a new targeting system. The eggs also bounce off of surfaces in the environment. Up to six eggs can be stored this way, and will trail behind the character. Yoshi can also eat certain items for power-up abilities. For instance, watermelons let Yoshi shoot seeds from his mouth like a machine gun, and fire enemies turn his mouth into a flamethrower. Other power-ups transform Yoshi into vehicles including cars, drills, helicopters, and submarines. A star power-up makes Baby Mario invulnerable and extra fast.
paragraph_selection.heading: Aiming eggs and transforming Yoshi

paragraph_selection.body: While Yoshi is "virtually invincible", if hit by an enemy, Baby Mario will float off his back in a bubble while a timer counts down to zero. When the timer expires, Koopas arrive to take Baby Mario and Yoshi loses a life. The player can replenish the timer by collecting small stars and power-ups. However, Yoshi can also lose a life instantly if he comes into contact with obstacles such as pits, spikes, lava, and thorns. Similar to Super Mario World, the player can hold a power-up in reserve, such as a "+10 star" (which adds ten seconds to the Baby Mario timer) or a "magnifying glass" (which reveals all hidden red coins in a level). These power-ups are acquired in several minigames. At the end of each level, the Yoshi relays Baby Mario to the successive Yoshi. If the player perfects all eight levels in each world by finishing with all flowers, red coins, and full 30 seconds on the timer, two hidden levels will unlock. There are three save slots on the cartridge.
paragraph_selection.heading: Recovering Baby Mario before time runs out

paragraph_selection.original: After four years of development, Yoshi's Island was released in Japan in August 1995 and worldwide two months later. It sold more than four million copies. Critics described it as one of the greatest video games of all time, praising the art, sound, level design and gameplay. The art style and Yoshi's signature characteristics established the Yoshi series of spin-offs and sequels.

Critics described it as one of the greatest video games of all time, praising the art, sound, level design and gameplay. The art style and Yoshi's signature characteristics established the Yoshi series of spin-offs and sequels.
paragraph_selection.heading: Release and reception

paragraph_selection.original: Yoshi's Island was the last Super Mario platformer before the series' transition to 3D gameplay, with no further 2D entries for over a decade. It was ported to the Game Boy Advance as Yoshi's Island: Super Mario Advance 3 in 2002; this version was rereleased for the Nintendo 3DS and the Wii U's Virtual Console. The original version was also released for the Super NES Classic Edition, and both versions for the Nintendo Classics service.

old_entry.summary: Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest  is a 1995 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).
body: Donkey Kong Country 2: Diddy's Kong Quest  is a 1995 platform game developed by Rare and published by Nintendo for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It was released on 21 November 1995 in Japan, 4 December in North America, and 14 December in Europe. It is the second installment of the Donkey Kong Country series and the sequel to Donkey Kong Country (1994). It was re-released for the Game Boy Advance (GBA) in 2004. The game was made available for download on the Virtual Console for the Wii and Wii U in 2007 and 2015, respectively.

Players control Diddy Kong and his girlfriend Dixie Kong, who must rescue Donkey Kong after he is kidnapped by King K. Rool. The game is set on Crocodile Isle, with eight worlds of varying environments, totaling 52 levels. The game uses the same Silicon Graphics (SGI) technology from the original, which features the use of pre-rendered 3D imagery. Diddy's Kong Quest received acclaim and is regarded as one of the greatest 2D platformers of all time. Praise was directed at its soundtrack, which is considered one of the greatest of all time, as well as its graphics and gameplay. It was the second best-selling game of 1995, and the sixth best-selling game on the SNES. It was followed by Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! in 1996.

old_entry.summary: Rave Racer is a 1995 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades.
body: Rave Racer is a 1995 racing video game developed and published by Namco for arcades. It is the third title in the Ridge Racer series and the follow-up to Ridge Racer and Ridge Racer 2. Rave Racer runs on Namco System 22 hardware, and could be played by two people per cabinet for up to eight players total when up to four of them were linked together. Compared to Ridge Racer 2, Rave Racer adds two new tracks as well as the ability to play the original two, various handling changes, force feedback steering, and improved car and racetrack graphics. Rave Racer was a critical and commercial success; it would be the last major arcade Ridge Racer title until Ridge Racer V: Arcade Battle (2000) as Namco focused on home consoles with titles such as R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 (1998) and Ridge Racer 64 (2000).

old_entry.title: Suikoden
old_entry.subtitle: A revolution needs many people
old_entry.summary: On December 15, 1995, Konami released Suikoden for PlayStation in Japan, beginning a series loosely inspired by the Chinese classic Shui Hu Zhuan, also known as Water Margin.
body: On December 15, 1995, Konami released Suikoden for PlayStation in Japan, beginning a series loosely inspired by the Chinese classic Shui Hu Zhuan, also known as Water Margin. The game builds its political scale through an unusual system: the protagonist can recruit 108 Stars of Destiny, many of whom are not simply fighters but people who materially transform the rebellion's base. The enormous cast does more than multiply portraits, because new arrivals open services, shops and functions. War is also represented at several levels, alternating traditional battles, duels and clashes between armies. Suikoden therefore speaks about revolution through organization, infrastructure and relationships, not only through the individual growth of the hero. Its identity comes from the idea that a political movement becomes visible as an empty fortress progressively fills with people.

Suikoden takes from Water Margin the idea of a large group of figures destined to converge around a rebellion. The 108 Stars of Destiny do not all carry the same narrative weight and do not all enter battle, but precisely this asymmetry makes the project believable. Some characters are warriors, while others open shops, services or activities at the base. Recruiting therefore changes how the space functions rather than merely completing a list. The player sees the revolution take shape through people with different skills. Konami would continue to regard this system as one of the series' distinctive traits, alongside Runes and large-scale battles. The strength of the first game lies in tying the desire for completion to a concrete consequence: every new arrival changes the appearance and possibilities of the army being built.

Many role-playing games represent growth through individual numbers. Suikoden adds a second scale: the Liberation Army's base changes as new people are recruited. Spaces that begin empty acquire functions, shops and activities, turning political progress into architecture. Konami still identifies base management as one of the series' characteristic systems. The fortress works because it is not simply a three-dimensional menu: the player can walk through it, meet characters and physically recognize what the group has built. Collective progression thus becomes perceptible without an abstract indicator. The enormous cast also gains a spatial justification, because many figures who do not join the active party remain present in the life of the rebellion. The base turns recruitment from quantity into community and gives concrete form to the idea of revolution.

Suikoden alternates party combat, duels and clashes between armies to represent the same political crisis at different scales. The system does not seek the depth of a complete wargame: instead, it conveys that the protagonist's decisions have moved beyond the scale of a single party. As the rebellion grows, the conflict can no longer be told only through six characters in formation. Army Battles translate alliances, losses and available forces into a broader language, while duels suddenly return everything to the personal reading of an opponent. Konami still cites these battles among the distinctive elements of the first game. The system's value therefore lies in its shift of perspective: the same story moves from the body of the individual to the structure of an army, reminding the player that a revolution is at once a private experience, a network of relationships and a military organization.

old_entry.title: Wipeout
old_entry.subtitle: The Future Takes on the Rhythm of the Night
old_entry.summary: On September 29, 1995, WipEout accompanied the European launch of the original PlayStation.
body: On September 29, 1995, WipEout accompanied the European launch of the original PlayStation. Sony remembers that date as the console's arrival in Europe and lists the Psygnosis game among the initial lineup. Developed in Liverpool, WipEout uses the possibilities of CD-ROM and 3D graphics to build anti-gravity races that demand anticipation, control of inertia and memory of the track. Its importance, however, goes beyond the driving model. Electronic music, art direction, graphic design and British club culture are treated as parts of the same project, giving the new console an image far removed from the idea of video games as children's toys. WipEout's future feels believable because it already seems to belong to the culture of 1995.

The project takes shape within Psygnosis's creative environment, with figures such as Nick Burcombe and Jim Bowers. The relationship between racing and electronic music does not arrive only as final packaging: it contributes to the idea of the experience itself. Rhythm has to support a sense of speed and concentration, making driving part of a broader identity. This relationship is interesting because it links a rule to a cultural context without requiring one to imitate the other literally. Music does not determine every corner, but it suggests the energy in which those corners are experienced. The game therefore seeks coherence between what the player does and what they hear, building a recognizable character before the audience has even learned every circuit.

The absence of wheels does not remove the weight of movement. The craft has to be steered with inertia and trajectory in mind, using air brakes in a way that makes anticipation important. Entering a corner badly can break speed and make recovery laborious. The first Wipeout is severe in this relationship with the track edges, and its difficulty belongs to the sensation of learning. The player has to stop correcting only what has already happened and begin preparing for the next passage. Speed therefore becomes a form of prediction. The circuit is learned through bodily memory until a sequence of obstacles becomes a line that can be travelled continuously.

Offensive tools add a direct relationship with other competitors, preventing the race from becoming only a solitary time trial. Using them requires attention to position and opportunity, while being hit can interrupt a carefully prepared trajectory. This interference makes the field more unstable without erasing the importance of driving. The player has to maintain concentration while the plan is disrupted. Futuristic racing therefore finds a balance between precision and conflict, with a tension different from that of a completely clean lap. The circuit remains a structure to learn, but it does not guarantee that every passage will repeat in the same way. The presence of other racers keeps part of the experience open even when the route is already known.

old_entry.title: Dragon Quest VI
old_entry.subtitle: Recognizing yourself between two worlds
old_entry.summary: On December 9, 1995, Dragon Quest VI: Maboroshi no Daichi was released in Japan for Super Famicom.
body: On December 9, 1995, Dragon Quest VI: Maboroshi no Daichi was released in Japan for Super Famicom. The game arrives at a point when the series can afford to expand its structure without abandoning the clarity that made it popular. The official theme is discovery: two overlapping worlds, uncertain identities and places whose meaning changes once the relationship between reality and dream is understood. Exploration is not used only to find the next objective, but to reconstruct a mental geography. The vocation system also returns, partly separating character growth from narrative identity and allowing abilities to be built through different paths. Dragon Quest VI therefore uses a traditional form to do something less linear: it asks the player to assemble scattered information, compare two maps and turn the journey into an exercise in recognition.

Dragon Quest VI's most recognizable structure is the movement between two worlds that share forms and names without matching perfectly. Square Enix officially describes the game's theme as discovery, and that idea becomes concrete in its geography. A place seen in one world can suggest a clue in the other; a seemingly complete town can gain a different meaning when the player understands which reality they are crossing. The map is therefore not merely a container for narrative stops, but a tool for comparison. Progress means remembering, connecting and returning with new knowledge. This structure makes exploration more active without giving up the visual clarity typical of the series. The player learns to question what is already familiar, turning familiarity itself into a source of doubt and new possibilities.

Dragon Quest VI brings back the vocation system and uses it to make growth less linear. Characters can learn abilities through different classes, building a mechanical history that does not completely coincide with their narrative role. Choosing a vocation changes priorities, statistics and access to abilities, but above all creates a relationship between invested time and specialization. Changing class does not erase what has been learned: the previous path remains readable in the character's repertoire. The system therefore encourages experimentation and planning without turning every decision into a permanent constraint. In a series known for the clarity of its rules, this flexibility adds depth while keeping the consequences understandable. Growth becomes a player-designed project, built battle after battle, rather than merely an automatic sequence of levels and statistics.

Square Enix also connects Dragon Quest VI to the theme of searching for oneself. The game does not address this idea only through dialogue and revelations, but distributes it across exploration, memory and progression. Characters move through worlds that reflect different possibilities, and the player must understand which relationships are real, dreamed or incomplete. The vocation system reinforces this ambiguity in an interesting way: a character has a precise narrative identity, but can assume different gameplay functions and accumulate abilities that do not depend on a single archetype. The system therefore does not simply illustrate the story, but echoes it. The question of who one is and what one can become is posed both by the narrative and by growth choices. It is an example of how a traditional JRPG can make theme and mechanics speak to each other without making them identical.

old_entry.title: Tales of Phantasia
old_entry.summary: Tales of Phantasia is an action role-playing video game developed by Wolf Team and published by Namco for the Super Famicom.
body: Tales of Phantasia is an action role-playing video game developed by Wolf Team and published by Namco for the Super Famicom. Originally released only in Japan in December 1995, it is the first title in the Tales series. It was later ported to a number of other platforms, including a Japan-exclusive version for the PlayStation in December 1998 and a Game Boy Advance version published by Namco in Japan in August 2003 and later published by Nintendo in North America and Europe in March 2006, which marked the first time the game was officially available in English. A PlayStation Portable remaster known as Tales of Phantasia Full Voice Edition followed in September 2006, featuring full voice acting during story scenes, which was later included with further enhancements as part of Tales of Phantasia: Narikiri Dungeon X in June 2010. The game's producers have given it the characteristic genre name Legendary RPG beginning with the PlayStation version, with the Full Voice Edition given the moniker Legendary RPG Embellished with Voices. An unofficial fan translation of the original Super Famicom version was released on February 12, 2001, by Dejap.

The game takes place in a fantasy world of Aselia and follows Cress Albane, a highly-trained swordsman who is driven by vengeance after his hometown is destroyed. Seeking further answers, he finds out that this is none other than a scheme to free the war-mongering Dhaos, the game's main antagonist. To prevent further catastrophes, Cress is aided by the use of time travel to gather allies from the past who can help him put an end to Dhaos's rampage in his own time.

The game was written and programmed by Yoshiharu Gotanda, designed by Masaki Norimoto, and scored by Motoi Sakuraba, Shinji Tamura and Ryota Furuya. The character designs were created by manga artist Kōsuke Fujishima. A short anime series based on the game, called Tales of Phantasia: The Animation, was released in 2004.

Tales of Phantasia experienced several delays and development challenges prior to its release in 1995, near the end of the Super Famicom's lifespan. It attracted attention due to its graphics, its original battle system, and its use of voice acting. It is also the first and only Super Famicom game to include an original, vocalized theme song. It sold over 1.3 million units in Japan alone, making it the second bestselling game in the franchise in that region, and one of the bestselling games in the franchise as a whole.
